## Part 1 · 00:02

[00:02] Second Temple Judaism is defined by two great catastrophes that punctuate [music] the history of the Jewish people in antiquity. The first of these was the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians in 586, and the second was the destruction by the Romans roughly 600 years later. Now, before the first destruction, Judah was a small kingdom but of several small kingdoms on the eastern shore of the Mediterranean. By the time the Romans came along, to be a Judahite or Judean was quite a different thing because Judeans were spread all over the eastern Mediterranean.

[00:51] So, it had also developed into a religion that was largely independent of the homeland. The homeland was important, and people cherished it, but when Jerusalem was destroyed the second time, Judaism could carry on. A first step that is, and a very basic one, was the establishing of the law of Moses as the authoritative law for Jews.

[01:41] Now, the law was, in one level, great unifying factor for Judaism, but it was also the source of division because people interpreted it in different ways, and so you get the rise of sectarianism, and out of that conflict arose a new world view, which we call apocalypticism. And where traditional Judaism had looked for a life where you would see your children and your children's children and live long in the land, now the hope was to live with the angels in heaven or in a new creation in a world [music] quite transformed.

[02:04] But the apocalyptic strand and the hellenistic strand also lived on because they were both vitally important to the offshoot of Judaism that was or became Christianity.
